question: How do DevOps, MLOps and LLMOps relate, and how are they applied to deploy and operate the LLM Twin pipelines (CI/CD, continuous training, prompt monitoring, alerting) on AWS?
contributions: Deployment of the LLM Twin pipelines to MongoDB, Qdrant, ZenML cloud and AWS (S3, ECR, SageMaker)
CI/CD with GitHub Actions, CT with ZenML, prompt monitoring with Opik, alerting with ZenML

limits: Tutorial for one stack (ZenML 0.64.0, Poetry 1.8.3, Python 3.11, AWS eu-central-1, GitHub Actions, Opik); UIs of MongoDB, Qdrant, ZenML will drift, authors say so.
No measurements: no latency, cost or quality numbers for CI/CD, CT or monitoring; GPT-4 figures are uncited and flagged unreliable.
Only a dummy test is implemented in CI; CT is a manual trigger with no drift detection; the CT pipeline is a monolith because of a free-trial limit; CD pushes to main only (no staging).
Authors are unsure the term LLMOps will last.
Allows MongoDB access from any IP, which they say is not safe for production.
practices: Start the orchestrator on day 0 even locally; it forces decoupled pipelines that exchange data only through storage (CT pipeline, p.36).
Order CI steps gitleaks, lint, format, then tests, since static checks are faster (p.27).
Put CI on pull requests and CD on pushes to the branch (main); tag images with commit SHA and latest (p.29-34).
Decouple dependency install from code copy in a Dockerfile to use layer caching (p.21).
Keep pipelines isolated and chain them with triggers rather than a monolith (p.39).
Build the manual deployment path first, then automate, to understand it for CI/CD debugging (p.22).
Use manual, REST API or scheduled triggers; once one command runs everything, adapt to advanced cases (p.37-38).
Add input and output guardrails and accept the latency trade-off; run retries in parallel and pick the best to limit latency (p.10).
Log full prompt traces with per-step latency, tokens and cost; trace the critical functions (rag, call_llm_service) first and add granularity as needed to avoid noise (p.11,42).
Monitor model configuration, total token counts and step duration; a sudden rise in average tokens signals a bug (p.43).
Add user feedback and LLM-judge scores to traces (p.41).
Send alerts on pipeline failure and success through the stack's alerter (p.43-44).
Set seeds and track code, data and hyperparameter versions for reproducibility (MLOps principles, p.7).
Most companies should choose a foundation model and optimise with prompt engineering, fine-tuning or RAG, not train from scratch (p.9).
